Title: The GOAT Debate: Analyzing Michael Jordan's Performance and Viewership Impact

Abstract:
The "Greatest of All Time" (GOAT) debate in basketball frequently centers around a few key players, most notably Michael Jordan, LeBron James, and Kobe Bryant. The main question this project aims to answer is: Who is objectively the greatest basketball player when analyzing both on-court performance statistics and off-court viewership impact? This specific report focuses on Michael Jordan, examining his career averages and the television viewership during his six NBA Finals appearances. Current preliminary results indicate that Jordan achieved an unparalleled combination of elite scoring (regularly exceeding 30 points per game) and massive global viewership draws, culminating in a historic 29 million average viewers during the 1998 NBA Finals.

Introduction:
The central question motivating this analysis is determining the greatest basketball player of all time based on empirical data rather than subjective opinion. This analysis benefits sports analysts, NBA historians, and fans who seek a data-driven approach to the GOAT debate. By testing the hypothesis that pure scoring dominance and peak viewership draw are the strongest indicators of a player's greatness, we aim to classify Michael Jordan's impact on the sport and eventually compare these findings to models of LeBron James and Kobe Bryant.

Executive Summary:

Michael Jordan was an elite scorer, averaging over 30 points per game during his first championship three-peat (1991-1993).

Viewership data indicates that Jordan's presence in the NBA Finals was an unprecedented television draw, peaking at an average of 29 million viewers during his final championship run in 1998.

His all-around impact is highlighted by his high volume of minutes played and reliable rebounding, demonstrating dominance on both ends of the floor.

Data:
The available data for this analysis includes a curated dataset (jordan_data.csv) tracking Michael Jordan's regular-season performance and Finals viewership over his six championship-winning seasons. The performance data was retrieved from publicly available NBA stat repositories (like Statmuse and Basketball Reference), and viewership data from sports media viewership archives (like Sports Media Watch). The dataset contains 6 observations across 6 variables: Season, Games Played, Points Per Game, Assists Per Game, Rebounds Per Game, and Finals Viewership in millions. Data cleaning involved formatting the variables properly into a CSV format and filtering specifically for his championship years to measure peak impact.

Visualization:
Preliminary visualizations will include a time-series line plot mapping Michael Jordan's "Points Per Game" alongside "Finals Viewership" to observe the relationship between his scoring volume and television ratings. Additionally, a scatter plot will be generated to analyze the consistency of his Rebounds and Assists alongside viewership peaks. These visualizations suggest that Jordan's sustained scoring output perfectly aligned with the steady growth in NBA Finals television ratings throughout the 1990s.

Analysis:
Moving forward, the analysis will utilize linear regression models to determine if there is a statistically significant correlation between Jordan's on-court performance metrics (Points/Assists/Rebounds) and the resulting Finals viewership numbers. We expect to find that his consistent high-level production established a baseline of unparalleled viewer interest. Ultimately, these models will be cross-referenced with identical models run for LeBron James and Kobe Bryant to definitively determine who had the highest statistical peak and the strongest absolute viewer pull.
